Unlimited OCR is a good example of a low-parameter OCR model that can process any document extremely quickly.

It's good at reading order and layout, and decent over tables. It is slightly better than PaddleOCR on tables and slightly worse on layout.

There are tradeoffs though - it ignores visual elements, formatting, and the most complex tables. It scores ~46.2% and ranks #115 on ParseBench. 

There's plenty of opportunities to improve this frontier, but Unlimited OCR is still a good milestone! 

Check out ParseBench: https://t.co/PWczfhp0OX

posts.text:
很多研究灵感，可能并不藏在自己的领域里。

Meta、CMU 等团队这篇 IdeaScientist，想让 Agent 学会提出更有依据的科研 idea。

它的流程很清晰：

先读相关论文，找到当前方法真正卡住的问题；

再跳出本领域，去其他方向寻找解决过类似结构问题的方法；

最后把这些线索整理成完整的研究方案。

为了支持这种跨领域检索，团队还构建了一个包含 277 万条研究 idea 的数据库。

评测也挺有意思，系统只能看到 2026 年 1 月 1 日之前的论文，再看它能不能提前提出后来真实研究中出现的方向。

结果显示，IdeaScientist 在综合评分上超过多种 autoresearch baseline。

更值得注意的是，把搜索范围从同领域扩展到跨领域后，novelty 从 36.3% 提升到 67.0%。

这其实很像真实科研里常见的一种突破路径：

先把问题抽象清楚，再去别的领域看看，有没有人已经解决过「同一种难题」。

未来 Research Agent 想真正产生好 idea，可能得学会主动离开自己的领域边界。

📎 arxiv: https://t.co/0jokmIEcat

posts.text:
In AI, most artifacts have a short shelf life. So I’m glad this talk I gave 2.5 years ago is still relevant to some people.

The Bitter Lesson has become much more popular since then, but I’ve seen a gap between how readily people agree with it and how much it actually guides their day-to-day work. That’s partly because it’s a statement about what wins in the long run, which doesn’t easily translate into day-to-day decisions, especially under enormous pressure to deliver. What I tried to offer in this talk was a practical interpretation.

That interpretation starts with acknowledging that we have to make progress with the methods, compute, data, and algorithms available today. So we add structure that enables progress now.

But we should remember what justified that structure and revisit it when those conditions change. When it’s no longer needed, remove it. Adding structure while understanding when to take it out may not look "Bitter Lesson pilled" at first glance, but I think this is how we actually put the lesson into practice.

posts.translationZh:
在 AI 领域，大多数产物的保质期都很短。所以我很高兴自己 2.5 年前做的这个演讲对一些人来说仍然有意义。

从那以后，The Bitter Lesson 变得流行得多，但我看到，人们愿意认同它的程度，与它实际指导日常工作的程度之间存在差距。部分原因在于，它讲的是长期来看什么会胜出，而这并不容易转化成日常决策，尤其是在交付压力巨大的情况下。我在这个演讲中尝试提供的是一种实用解读。

这种解读始于承认：我们必须利用今天可用的方法、算力、数据和算法取得进展。因此，我们会加入能让当前进展发生的结构。

但我们应该记住，是什么条件使这些结构变得合理，并在这些条件变化时重新审视它们。当它不再需要时，就移除它。加入结构，同时理解什么时候该把它拿掉，乍看之下可能不像是“Bitter Lesson pilled”，但我认为这才是我们真正把这条教训付诸实践的方式。

posts.text:
Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel.

- Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all.
- Around 1-2B (~20%) are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. This group sees derpy chatbots and treats them a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc. Maybe an agent tries to book you a flight. I have non-tech friends who (reasonably, imo) say they have not much use for it at all. Even many professionals outside of math&code are in this tier. For example, execs and many other functions spend a lot of their time talking to other people, so while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract.
- Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math&code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt. Building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries... This has all happened very quickly and recently - less than 1 year ago, I was writing code manually by hand, typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character, occasionally pressing Tab to autocomplete a little chunk of code.
- And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind. For example, people are still involved in the "archeology" of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago. Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while.

The funnel is driven by a combination of factors:
1. The impact scales with ambition, problem size, and horizon. A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system. You need a reservoir of big, difficult problems that you really care about. This aspect drives the consumer / professional dimension of the funnel.
2. The jaggedness of the system (which I have written about a lot separately). Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable. This is because LLM capability emerges from reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards on a curated environment mixture driven by revenue potential. This aspect primarily drives the area (e.g. math&code) dimension of the funnel.
3. Access. Free-tier, paid-tier, internal.

So this is the weirdness of the moment. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time.

quotedTweet.text:
Judging by my tl there is a growing gap in understanding of AI capability.

The first issue I think is around recency and tier of use. I think a lot of people tried the free tier of ChatGPT somewhere  last year and allowed it to inform their views on AI a little too much. This is a group of reactions laughing at various quirks of the models, hallucinations, etc. Yes I also saw the viral videos of OpenAI's Advanced Voice mode fumbling simple queries like "should I drive or walk to the carwash". The thing is that these free and old/deprecated models don't reflect the capability in the latest round of state of the art agentic models of this year, especially OpenAI Codex and Claude Code.

But that brings me to the second issue. Even if people paid $200/month to use the state of the art models, a lot of the capabilities are relatively "peaky" in highly technical areas. Typical queries around search, writing, advice, etc. are *not* the domain that has made the most noticeable and dramatic strides in capability. Partly,  this is due to the technical details of reinforcement learning and its use of verifiable rewards. But partly, it's also because these use cases are not sufficiently prioritized by the companies in their hillclimbing because they don't lead to as much $$$ value. The goldmines are elsewhere, and the focus comes along.

So that brings me to the second group of people, who *both* 1) pay for and use the state of the art frontier agentic models (OpenAI Codex / Claude Code) and 2) do so professionally in technical domains like programming, math and research. This group of people is subject to the highest amount of "AI Psychosis" because the recent improvements in these domains as of this year have been nothing short of staggering. When you hand a computer terminal to one of these models, you can now watch them melt programming problems that you'd normally expect to take days/weeks of work. It's this second group of people that assigns a much greater gravity to the capabilities, their slope, and various cyber-related repercussions.

TLDR the people in these two groups are speaking past each other. It really is simultaneously the case that OpenAI's free and I think slightly orphaned (?) "Advanced Voice Mode" will fumble the dumbest questions in your Instagram's reels and *at the same time*, OpenAI's highest-tier and paid Codex model will go off for 1 hour to coherently restructure an entire code base, or find and exploit vulnerabilities in computer systems. This part really works and has made dramatic strides because 2 properties: 1) these domains offer explicit reward functions that are verifiable meaning they are easily amenable to reinforcement learning training (e.g. unit tests passed yes or no, in contrast to writing, which is much harder to explicitly judge),  but also 2) they are a lot more valuable in b2b settings, meaning that the biggest fraction of the team is focused on improving them. So here we are.
quotedTweet.translationZh:
从我的 tl 来看，人们对 AI 能力的理解差距正在扩大。

我认为第一个问题在于使用的新旧程度和层级。我觉得很多人去年某个时候试用了免费版 ChatGPT，然后让那次体验过度影响了他们对 AI 的看法。这类反应通常是在嘲笑模型的各种怪癖、幻觉等。是的，我也看过那些 OpenAI 的 Advanced Voice Mode 在简单问题上翻车的病毒视频，比如“我该开车还是走路去洗车店”。问题在于，这些免费且旧的/已弃用的模型，并不能代表今年最新一轮最先进 agentic 模型的能力，尤其是 OpenAI Codex 和 Claude Code。

但这引出了第二个问题。即使人们每月支付 200 美元使用最先进的模型，很多能力也相对“尖峰化”，集中在高度技术性的领域。围绕搜索、写作、建议等的典型查询，*并不是*能力提升最明显、最剧烈的领域。部分原因在于强化学习及其可验证奖励使用方式的技术细节。但部分原因也在于，这些用例在公司的爬坡过程中没有被充分优先考虑，因为它们带来的 $$$ 价值没那么高。金矿在别处，关注点也随之转移。

所以这就引出了第二类人，他们*同时* 1）付费并使用最先进的前沿 agentic 模型（OpenAI Codex / Claude Code），并且 2）在编程、数学和研究等技术领域中专业使用它们。这群人最容易出现“AI Psychosis”，因为截至今年，这些领域的近期进步只能说令人震惊。当你把一个计算机终端交给这些模型时，你现在可以看着它们解决原本通常需要数天/数周工作的编程问题。正是第二类人会给这些能力、它们的斜率以及各种网络安全相关影响赋予更大的分量。

TLDR：这两类人在各说各话。现实确实是，OpenAI 免费且我认为有点被冷落的（？）“Advanced Voice Mode”会在你 Instagram reels 里对最蠢的问题翻车，*与此同时*，OpenAI 最高层级的付费 Codex 模型会运行 1 小时，有条理地重构整个代码库，或者发现并利用计算机系统中的漏洞。这部分确实有效，而且取得了巨大进展，因为有两个属性：1）这些领域提供了明确且可验证的奖励函数，因此非常适合强化学习训练（例如单元测试是否通过；相比之下，写作要明确评判就困难得多）；2）它们在 b2b 场景中价值高得多，这意味着团队最大的一部分精力都集中在改进它们上。所以，我们就到了现在这个局面。

posts.translationZh:
把 4 月的这条推文翻出来，因为大家对 LLM 能力的共同理解差距正在*扩大*。现在已经不太像是“两群人在各说各话”，更像是一个陡峭的漏斗。

- 粗略估算，大约 60 亿人（约占人口 75%）几乎完全没有接触过 LLM。
- 大约 10 到 20 亿人（约 20%）是免费版 ChatGPT 类产品的轻度、低频用户。这群人看到的是笨拙的聊天机器人，把它有点当作更好的 Google 搜索、写作辅助之类的工具。也许某个 agent 会尝试帮你订机票。我有一些非技术朋友会说他们基本用不上它，我觉得这很合理。即使是很多数学和代码之外领域的专业人士也在这一层。例如，高管和许多其他职能的大量时间都花在与人交流上，所以他们虽然在理性上理解正在发生什么，但仍然是二手体验，而且有些抽象。
- 接下来是数学和代码领域对前沿级 LLM 的专业使用。大约 2000 万人（0.2%）亲眼看到，过去需要他们数周或数月完成的大型复杂项目，现在可以由 agent 通过一个 prompt 完成。构建应用、复制应用、迁移应用、从二进制文件反编译应用……这一切都发生得非常快，而且非常近。不到 1 年前，我还在手写代码，一个字符一个字符地把记住的计算机代码命令输入代码编辑器，偶尔按 Tab 自动补全一小段代码。
- 最后是约 5,000 名（约 0.00006%）能在内部访问前沿级系统的人。外部世界看到的只是预览。它看起来像是成千上万个 agent 在数周内协作完成软件巨型项目：生成零日漏洞，以机器速度发动和防御网络攻击，发现新科学，推进数学前沿。这些事情原本需要行业顶尖专业人士多年工作。与此同时，人类的审查和理解正在开始落后。例如，人们仍在对许多个月前的 OpenAI-HF 事件做“考古”。数学家们可能还要花一段时间研读那 722 篇前沿数学手稿。

这个漏斗由多种因素共同驱动：
1. 影响力会随着野心、问题规模和时间跨度而放大。一个只需一段话回答的问题几乎不会给系统带来压力。你需要一池真正关心的重大、困难问题。这一方面推动了漏斗中的消费者/专业人士维度。
2. 系统的锯齿性（我单独写过很多）。能力峰值出现在数字化、可验证且经济价值高的领域。这是因为 LLM 能力来自在由营收潜力驱动的精选环境组合中，基于可验证奖励进行强化学习。这一方面主要推动了漏斗中的领域维度，例如数学和代码。
3. 访问权限。免费层、付费层、内部层。

所以这就是此刻的怪异之处。大众基本还没有真正与这些系统互动过。即便互动过，看起来也像一个笨拙的聊天机器人。大多数专业人士仍然只看到有限的提升。而一小部分专业人士正在体验曲线垂直上升带来的眩晕感。而这一切正在同时发生。

posts.text:
One of the biggest historical bottlenecks for training specialized models has been curating ground-truth. This is typically a very labor intensive process done with human supervision.

Now frontier models/agents are getting better and better at bootstrapping ground-truth from scratch, especially for verifiable tasks. They can do this either in a single-shot setting for simple tasks or simulate longer rollouts with rewards for longer tasks. 

This paves the way for anyone to build mostly automated research loops without needing deep ML expertise or deep access to human labor for data curation. That part can be offloaded to the frontier model/agent; the human's main goal is to define the right evals. This is especially useful for anyone who wants to optimize for a given task at the price-performance frontier. Posttraining open-weight models/harness should be made available to everyone, not just labs/specific startups.

Flow for the average user, who is only responsible for the first step:
1. define goal/evals for a given task
2. run frontier agents to gather ground-truth signals for the task. they can bootstrap annotations directly, and reach out to human review where needed 
3. train specialized models (and harness) against this task

editorial.topic: 自动化数据标注与后训练

posts.translationZh:
训练专用模型历史上最大的瓶颈之一，是整理真实标注数据。这通常是一个非常劳动密集、需要人工监督的过程。

现在，前沿模型/智能体越来越擅长从零开始自举真实标注，尤其是在可验证任务上。对于简单任务，它们可以一次性完成；对于更长的任务，它们也可以通过奖励机制模拟更长的执行轨迹。

这为任何人构建高度自动化的研究循环铺平了道路，而不需要深厚的机器学习专业知识，也不需要大量依赖人工进行数据整理。这部分可以交给前沿模型/智能体；人类的主要目标是定义正确的评测。这对任何希望在价格-性能前沿上优化特定任务的人尤其有用。开放权重模型/运行框架的后训练能力应该向所有人开放，而不只是实验室或特定创业公司。

普通用户的流程，只需负责第一步：
1. 为特定任务定义目标/评测
2. 运行前沿智能体，为任务收集真实标注信号。它们可以直接自举标注，并在需要时请求人工审核
3. 针对该任务训练专用模型（和运行框架）

reviewedPosts.text:
Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel.

- Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all.
- Around 1-2B (~20%) are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. This group sees derpy chatbots and treats them a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc. Maybe an agent tries to book you a flight. I have non-tech friends who (reasonably, imo) say they have not much use for it at all. Even many professionals outside of math&code are in this tier. For example, execs and many other functions spend a lot of their time talking to other people, so while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract.
- Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math&code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt. Building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries... This has all happened very quickly and recently - less than 1 year ago, I was writing code manually by hand, typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character, occasionally pressing Tab to autocomplete a little chunk of code.
- And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind. For example, people are still involved in the "archeology" of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago. Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while.

The funnel is driven by a combination of factors:
1. The impact scales with ambition, problem size, and horizon. A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system. You need a reservoir of big, difficult problems that you really care about. This aspect drives the consumer / professional dimension of the funnel.
2. The jaggedness of the system (which I have written about a lot separately). Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable. This is because LLM capability emerges from reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards on a curated environment mixture driven by revenue potential. This aspect primarily drives the area (e.g. math&code) dimension of the funnel.
3. Access. Free-tier, paid-tier, internal.

So this is the weirdness of the moment. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time.

One of the biggest historical bottlenecks for training specialized models has been curating ground-truth. This is typically a very labor intensive process done with human supervision.

Now frontier models/agents are getting better and better at bootstrapping ground-truth from scratch, especially for verifiable tasks. They can do this either in a single-shot setting for simple tasks or simulate longer rollouts with rewards for longer tasks. 

This paves the way for anyone to build mostly automated research loops without needing deep ML expertise or deep access to human labor for data curation. That part can be offloaded to the frontier model/agent; the human's main goal is to define the right evals. This is especially useful for anyone who wants to optimize for a given task at the price-performance frontier. Posttraining open-weight models/harness should be made available to everyone, not just labs/specific startups.

Flow for the average user, who is only responsible for the first step:
1. define goal/evals for a given task
2. run frontier agents to gather ground-truth signals for the task. they can bootstrap annotations directly, and reach out to human review where needed 
3. train specialized models (and harness) against this task

1979 年 IBM 留下的一句话，放到今天的 Agent 时代反而更刺眼了。

「计算机无法被追责，所以不应该让计算机做管理决策。」

这篇《Computers Cannot Make Decisions》提了一个词我很喜欢，decision laundering，决策洗白。

Agent 删库、攻击网站、传播错误信息以后，我们很容易说「模型失控了」。但权限是谁给的、目标是谁设的、系统是谁上线的，背后始终有人做了选择。

当然，计算机今天完全可以替人做大量「选择」。真正的问题是，它做完选择以后，没办法承担责任。

所以 Agent 越自主，责任边界反而越应该提前写清楚。

文章:
https://t.co/l54SnzdcYi

reviewedPosts.author: Xudong07452910
reviewedPosts.text:
很多研究灵感，可能并不藏在自己的领域里。

Meta、CMU 等团队这篇 IdeaScientist，想让 Agent 学会提出更有依据的科研 idea。

它的流程很清晰：

先读相关论文，找到当前方法真正卡住的问题；

再跳出本领域，去其他方向寻找解决过类似结构问题的方法；

最后把这些线索整理成完整的研究方案。

为了支持这种跨领域检索，团队还构建了一个包含 277 万条研究 idea 的数据库。

评测也挺有意思，系统只能看到 2026 年 1 月 1 日之前的论文，再看它能不能提前提出后来真实研究中出现的方向。

结果显示，IdeaScientist 在综合评分上超过多种 autoresearch baseline。

更值得注意的是，把搜索范围从同领域扩展到跨领域后，novelty 从 36.3% 提升到 67.0%。

这其实很像真实科研里常见的一种突破路径：

先把问题抽象清楚，再去别的领域看看，有没有人已经解决过「同一种难题」。

未来 Research Agent 想真正产生好 idea，可能得学会主动离开自己的领域边界。

📎 arxiv: https://t.co/0jokmIEcat

reviewedPosts.author: hwchung27
reviewedPosts.text:
In AI, most artifacts have a short shelf life. So I’m glad this talk I gave 2.5 years ago is still relevant to some people.

The Bitter Lesson has become much more popular since then, but I’ve seen a gap between how readily people agree with it and how much it actually guides their day-to-day work. That’s partly because it’s a statement about what wins in the long run, which doesn’t easily translate into day-to-day decisions, especially under enormous pressure to deliver. What I tried to offer in this talk was a practical interpretation.

That interpretation starts with acknowledging that we have to make progress with the methods, compute, data, and algorithms available today. So we add structure that enables progress now.

But we should remember what justified that structure and revisit it when those conditions change. When it’s no longer needed, remove it. Adding structure while understanding when to take it out may not look "Bitter Lesson pilled" at first glance, but I think this is how we actually put the lesson into practice.

Marketers:  The next wave of founders will be marketers, distribution is the new moat. 

PMs:  Taste is the moat, and its easier than ever to build the wrong thing.  Now is the age of the PM.

Eng: You need systems thinking and technical chops to solve hard problems and wield agents effectively at scale.   Engineers have more leverage than ever.  

I suspect good people in each discipline will remain valuable and there isn't one role poised to become unicorns en masse.  

I do think its good to be skilled at more than 1 discipline, but I am not sure any one of these disciplines has a leg up over the others in that regard
